newsitem.title: USA: NYC Indep. Budget sees slowing securities industry.
newsitem.headline: NYC Indep. Budget sees slowing securities industry.

text.p: New York City's Independent Budget Office said Friday the securities industry, the main engine that pulled its economy up, will slow but stay positive in the next few years as profits slip from record levels.

In its first fiscal outlook, the body, which was designed to serve the same role as the Congressional Budget Office does for the federal government, also predicted that job growth in 1997 would only be about 0.3 percent, less than half the 0.7 percent rise seen in the previous year.

Profits by Wall Street brokerages and banks have soared with the Dow Jones Industrial Average, but as this sector's earnings ease, one of the most direct effects will be seen in the city's collection of personal income taxes.
In fiscal 1997, tax collections for both the city and the state were boosted by the over $8 billion of bonuses these firms were estimated to have paid their employees.

The Independent Budget Office sees growth in the city's personal income taxes falling to 3.6 percent in 1997 from 4.5 percent in 1996. After that, it should start firming again, however, with a rise of 3.8 percent forecast for 1998.
And by 2001, New Yorkers are expected to be paying 4.9 percent more in personal income taxes.

The costs of two of the biggest components of the city's budget -- welfare and Medicaid -- are anticipated to head in opposite directions, with welfare spending forecast to fall by $100 million to about $1.48 billion in 1998. The amount spent on this program is predicted to decline gradually to $1.4 billion in 2001.

New York City's share of the state Home Relief program is only expected to rise by a slim $8 million in 1998 to $567 million, though by 2001, these expenditures will hit $610 million, the Independent Budget Office found.

But spending on Medicaid, which helps pay for healthcare for the needy, was forecast to rise by $110 million to $2.19 billion in 1998, despite state and federal efforts to contain costs. Assuming a 4.2 percent growth rate, this program will cost New York City $2.5 billion in 2001.
